h1: Electrical Panel Upgrades and Replacement in Broward County
intro: When your electrical panel is worn out or unsafe, everything downstream of it is at risk. A panel is the heart of your electrical system, and it usually lets you know when it is failing: breakers that trip for no clear reason, a burning smell, scorch marks near the cover, lights that dim when the air conditioner kicks on. Sometimes there is no warning at all, and the first sign is a letter from your insurance company. Here in South Florida, carriers are refusing to cover homes with obsolete panels, and 4-point inspections are failing them every day. We replace a panel once, we price it right, and we handle the permit and the inspector for you. And if your panel is safe and current, we will tell you that too.

definition.heading: What an electrical panel upgrade is
definition.body: An electrical panel upgrade is the removal of your old load center and the installation of a modern one built to today's code. The panel is where power from the utility is divided into the circuits that feed your home or building. Over the years, panels wear out, run short on space, or come from an era whose equipment the industry no longer considers safe. An upgrade replaces the panel, the breakers, and often the connections and grounding that go with it, so the whole system works the way it should. For many South Florida property owners the trigger is insurance, because carriers now decline or drop coverage over outdated equipment. Whatever brings you to it, the result is a service that is safe, current, and insurable again.

symptoms.title: Your insurer or inspector flagged it
symptoms.body: Your carrier sent a notice, or a 4-point inspection called out the panel. In South Florida this is the most common reason people call us. The company will not renew until the equipment is brought up to a modern, insurable standard.

symptoms.title: Breakers trip for no clear reason
symptoms.body: Breakers trip often, or one refuses to reset. A breaker that will not hold is telling you something downstream is wrong, or the breaker itself is worn out. Either way, it is a sign the panel is no longer doing its job.

symptoms.title: You smell burning or see scorch marks
symptoms.body: You notice a burning smell, scorch marks, or discoloration around the panel cover. That is heat where there should be none. It usually means a connection is failing, and it deserves a look before it gets any worse.

symptoms.title: Lights dim when big appliances start
symptoms.body: Lights flicker or dim when the air conditioner or a large appliance turns on. An occasional flicker can be minor, but a steady pattern often points to a panel that can no longer carry the load it is being asked to carry.

symptoms.title: You have a fuse box or a flagged brand
symptoms.body: You still have an old fuse box, or a panel from a brand insurers flag, such as Zinsco or Federal Pacific. Older equipment was built for a lighter electrical life than your home lives today, and carriers know these names by heart. The brand alone, not a symptom, is often what an inspector reacts to.

symptoms.title: The panel is warm or buzzing
symptoms.body: The panel feels warm to the touch, or you hear a buzz coming from inside it. Electricity is something we do not see, we only feel the effect. Warmth and sound are two effects worth taking seriously before they grow.

localSections.heading: South Florida homes and the panels inside them
localSections.body: Broward County housing was built across many decades, and every era left its own electrical fingerprint. Homes from the middle of the last century often still carry fuse boxes or early breaker panels sized for a much lighter electrical life. Homes from later decades frequently hold panel brands the industry no longer considers safe. Newer construction is generally well protected, which is exactly why the older stock stands out to inspectors and carriers. The climate does not help. Constant heat keeps components warm even at rest, humidity finds its way into enclosures, and homes near the coast deal with salt air that quietly corrodes the lugs, bus bars, and terminations inside a panel. A connection that has loosened or corroded runs hotter than it should, and heat is the enemy of a panel, which is why equipment down here can age faster than the same panel would in a drier, cooler place. When we open a panel during an assessment, the condition of the connections tells us a great deal about how much life is left in it.

localSections.heading: Why carriers are driving so many upgrades
localSections.body: The insurance market in South Florida has tightened, and outdated electrical equipment is one of the first things carriers look at. A 4-point inspection reports on the roof, plumbing, HVAC, and electrical, and an obsolete panel is a common reason the electrical section fails. Some carriers decline new policies over it, and others drop existing customers at renewal. This is honest, verifiable reality, and it is why a homeowner who never worried about the panel suddenly has a deadline. We describe it calmly because there is no need to dramatize it. The path forward is straightforward: replace the equipment with a modern, code-compliant panel, pass the inspection, and the electrical objection goes away. We pull the permit, and we are the ones who meet the inspector on site, so nothing gets lost in translation. We have walked many South Florida property owners through exactly that, and we can walk you through it too.

guide.title: The complete guide to upgrading your electrical panel in South Florida

sections.heading: What a panel upgrade actually is
sections.body: Your electrical panel is the point where power from the utility enters your property and gets divided into the individual circuits that feed your lights, outlets, and appliances. People call it the panel, the breaker box, the load center, or the fuse box, and they are all talking about the same thing. A panel upgrade is the removal of that old equipment and the installation of a modern replacement built to today's code. Depending on the property, an upgrade can be just the panel itself, or it can include the breakers, the grounding, the connections, and the way the panel ties into the rest of the service. The goal is simple: a panel that is the right size for how the property actually uses power, wired with connections that run cool, protected by breakers that trip the moment they are supposed to. When the heart of the system is sound, everything downstream of it is safer. Electricity is something we do not see, we only feel the effect, so the work of a good panel is quiet and invisible. You notice it most when it is missing.

sections.heading: When a panel can simply stay
sections.body: Not every aging panel needs to be replaced, and we will never tell you it does when it does not. If your existing panel is a safe, current brand with room to spare, we are not going to talk you into replacing it. We stay in our lane and we do not sell work that does not need doing. When a panel is worn, obsolete, or unsafe, we will say so plainly and show you what we see during the assessment, whether that is heat damage, a failing connection, a full panel with no room, or a brand carriers no longer accept. When it is fine and has years left, we will tell you that too, and you can call us again when something actually changes. That honesty is a big part of why customers keep coming back and sending their neighbors after ten years.

sections.heading: The panels insurers flag: Zinsco, Federal Pacific, and old fuse boxes
sections.body: A handful of older panel types come up again and again when carriers and 4-point inspections flag a home, and it helps to know the names. Zinsco panels and Federal Pacific panels, the ones whose breakers are often labeled Stab-Lok, are both obsolete brands with a documented history: their breakers can fail to trip under a fault, which is the one job a breaker has. Old fuse boxes are the other common flag, built for a much lighter electrical life than a modern home lives. Because these brands are obsolete, genuine parts are hard to source and a real repair is usually not practical, so replacement is the honest answer rather than a patch. Insurance carriers in South Florida know all three by name, which is why many owners learn what they have from a renewal notice or an inspection rather than any obvious symptom. If this is your situation, it is familiar ground for us, and it has a clean, well understood fix: a modern, code-compliant panel that passes inspection and removes the objection tied to the brand.

sections.heading: The day of the work and an honest conversation about cost
sections.body: A panel replacement is a focused, one-visit job for our crew in most homes. We coordinate with the utility so power to the property can be interrupted safely for the work window, then our in-house crew removes the old panel, sets the new one, and reconnects every circuit, labeling as we go so you end up with a panel you can actually read. We check and correct the grounding and the terminations, because a new panel is only as good as the connections feeding it. You will be without power for part of the day, and we tell you honestly ahead of time so you can plan around it. On cost, a panel upgrade is quoted per property after an on-site assessment, because the number depends on the condition of the service, the grounding, and the size the property needs. Our service call is $240, which covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis, and if the problem can be handled on the spot there is no separate return charge. For the replacement itself, we forecast what the job takes and give you one price before we begin, and that price does not change mid-job. Price it once, price it right. If a panel upgrade turns out to be part of a larger service rebuild, we will show you exactly where one job ends and the other begins, and we will price each scope on its own.

sections.heading: How to choose the right contractor
sections.body: A panel sits at the center of your home's safety, so the contractor who replaces it matters as much as the panel itself. Start with licensing. Ghost Crown Electric is a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor with statewide authority and a Broward County Master Electrician, with 286 permitted projects on public record. Ask who actually does the work, because a rotating crew of subcontractors is not the same as an in-house team that has worked together for years. Ask who attends the inspection, because when the team that priced the job is the team that meets the inspector, details do not fall through the cracks. Ask how they price, since a contractor who forecasts the job and holds the number is telling you they understand the work. And be careful of anyone who wins by talking down every other company. We do not do that. We stay in our lane, we let the license and the record speak, and we give a customer more than what they pay for.

faqs.answer: Send us the notice or the 4-point report and we will read it with you. In most cases the fix is a modern, code-compliant panel that passes inspection. We come out, assess the service in person, quote the replacement per property, pull the permit, and we meet the inspector so the sign-off is clean and your carrier's objection goes away.

faqs.question: How much does a panel upgrade cost?
faqs.answer: A panel upgrade is quoted per property after an on-site assessment, because the number depends on the condition of the service, the grounding, and the size your property needs. Our service call is $240, covering roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis. Once we see it, we forecast the job and give you one honest price that does not change mid-job.

faqs.question: I have a Zinsco or Federal Pacific panel. Do I have to replace it?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, and we will tell you straight why. These are obsolete brands with a documented history of breakers that can fail to trip under a fault, which is why carriers and 4-point inspections react to the name, and genuine parts are hard to source, so a real repair is rarely practical. Old fuse boxes fall in the same group. That said, if your panel is a safe, current brand with room to spare, we will not talk you into replacing it. We only recommend work that needs doing.

faqs.question: Do I really need a permit for this?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you want one. A permit puts a licensed contractor and a county inspector between you and a costly mistake, and it documents that the work was done to current code. We pull the permit as part of the job, schedule the inspection, and we meet the inspector on site in person, so nothing about the sign-off is left to chance.

faqs.question: Will my power be off during the work?
faqs.answer: For part of the day, yes. Replacing a panel means the power feeding it has to be interrupted safely while we work. We tell you honestly ahead of time what to expect so you can plan around it, and because our in-house crew does this work constantly, it is a focused, in and out type of situation rather than a job that drags on.

faqs.question: How long does a panel upgrade take?
faqs.answer: Most residential panel replacements are a focused, one-visit job for our crew, though the exact timing depends on what we find during the assessment. We will give you a realistic window when we quote the work, and we will not promise a specific timeline before we have seen the service in person. Every electrical situation is a little different, and the site visit comes first.
